Image caption,
Lostprophets singer Ian Watkins accepted he was a 'determined and committed paedophile'
**Ian Watkins, singer of Welsh rock band Lostprophets, has pleaded guilty to a series of "depraved" child sex offences including attempted rape of a baby.**
He had previously "furiously denied" the allegations.
The 36-year-old from Pontypridd and two women had been due to stand trial at Cardiff Crown Court.
Watkins pleaded guilty to attempted rape and sexual assault of a child under 13 but not guilty to rape. This was accepted by the prosecution.
Sentencing will take place on 18 December.
Prosecuting barrister Chris Clee QC told the court: "Ian Watkins was the lead singer in a successful band called the Lostprophets.
"He accepts he was a determined and committed paedophile."
Watkins also admitted conspiring to rape a child, three counts of sexual assault involving children, seven involving taking, making or possessing indecent images of children and one of possessing an extreme pornographic image involving a sex act on an animal.
The evidence against the defendant came from computers, laptops and mobile phones.
One laptop seized from Watkins's home was password protected with an obscenity relating to sexual activity with children, which was uncovered when it was sent to GCHQ to be cracked.
The court heard that he filmed and kept the episodes of abuse - which took place in various hotels in London and south Wales - which were recovered by police. Some of the evidence was too extreme and distressing to report.
Figure caption,
Catrin Evans from the Crown Prosecution Service and Chief Inspector Peter Doyle from South Wales Police
Referring to two women standing alongside Watkins in the dock, Mr Clee said: "Both women sexually abused their own children and made them available to Watkins for him to abuse."
The court was told how the abuse of the children by all parties was also evident in text messages.
Watkins sent a text to one of the women saying: "If you belong to me, so does your baby."
In an exchange involving the other woman, she sent Watkins a message along with an image of her child to the effect that her child needed to know she was not loved.

# Lostprophets' Ian Watkins guilty of child sex offences
Watkins also planned to "teach" the babies how to take drugs, the hearing was told.
Mr Clee said drugs played "a significant part in his offending against children".
Police found meth, cocaine and GHB during their searches.
Mr Clee told the court drugs were a "regular theme" in his dealings with the two other defendants.
Claiming his innocence, Watkins had told police during interviews he was being stalked by "a crazed fan" and other people had access to his computers.
He claimed he was the "victim of a malicious campaign".
The court heard in Oct 2006, Watkins met up in a hotel with a 16-year-old girl from Boston, who he had met during during a Lostprophets concert.
She dressed in a schoolgirl's outfit and he filmed their encounter.
In Oct 2008 he filmed himself having sex with another 16-year-old girl, who was also a Lostprophets fan.

# Lostprophets' Ian Watkins guilty of child sex offences
## Exploited status
One of the two women charged alongside Watkins, Woman A, admitted the attempted rape of a baby after denying rape and two charges of sexual assault as well as taking and distributing an indecent photograph of a child.
Woman B pleaded guilty to conspiring to rape a child, three sexual assault charges and four charges of taking, possessing or distributing indecent images.
After hearing legal argument from barristers, Mr Justice Royce called the jury into court and told them: "There will not be a trial in this case. The defendants have all pleaded guilty to nearly all the charges against them. The prosecution does not seek a trial in these circumstances.
"You have been saved from having to watch extremely graphic and distressing material."
Mr Clee told the judge there had been an argument regarding what some key video evidence showed.
"From the footage, there is an argument as to whether the full offence (of rape) is made out," he told judge Mr Justice Royce.
"If it is made out, it is minimal. There is so little difference between the full attempt and the attempt as to make no difference."
Image caption,
Watkins founded Lostprophets in 1997
Sally O'Neill, defending Watkins, said the singer was under the care of a psychiatrist.
Speaking outside the court, Det Ch Insp Peter Doyle from South Wales Police said: "This investigation has uncovered the most shocking and harrowing child abuse evidence I have ever seen.
"There is no doubt in my mind that Ian Watkins exploited his celebrity status in order to abuse young children.
"Today's outcome ensures the three people responsible have been brought to justice."
"Two very young children have been removed from this abuse and given a future that would otherwise have been denied them.
"The investigation has been extremely complex and challenging with key information and evidence being identified from witnesses worldwide."
He added that today's guilty pleas did not mark the end of the investigation and the force would work "tirelessly" to identify other victims or witnesses.
Lostprophets guitarist Lee Gaze expressed his relief on Twitter that the case had been concluded, writing: "That was over quick.... Thanks for the kind words. At least there is closure now."

Image caption,
Lostprophets singer Ian Watkins accepted he was a 'determined and committed paedophile'
**Ian Watkins, singer of Welsh rock band Lostprophets, has pleaded guilty to a series of "depraved" child sex offences including attempted rape of a baby.**
He had previously "furiously denied" the allegations.
The 36-year-old from Pontypridd and two women had been due to stand trial at Cardiff Crown Court.
Watkins pleaded guilty to attempted rape and sexual assault of a child under 13 but not guilty to rape. This was accepted by the prosecution.
Sentencing will take place on 18 December.
Prosecuting barrister Chris Clee QC told the court: "Ian Watkins was the lead singer in a successful band called the Lostprophets.
"He accepts he was a determined and committed paedophile."
Watkins also admitted conspiring to rape a child, three counts of sexual assault involving children, seven involving taking, making or possessing indecent images of children and one of possessing an extreme pornographic image involving a sex act on an animal.
The evidence against the defendant came from computers, laptops and mobile phones.
One laptop seized from Watkins's home was password protected with an obscenity relating to sexual activity with children, which was uncovered when it was sent to GCHQ to be cracked.
The court heard that he filmed and kept the episodes of abuse - which took place in various hotels in London and south Wales - which were recovered by police. Some of the evidence was too extreme and distressing to report.
Figure caption,
Catrin Evans from the Crown Prosecution Service and Chief Inspector Peter Doyle from South Wales Police
Referring to two women standing alongside Watkins in the dock, Mr Clee said: "Both women sexually abused their own children and made them available to Watkins for him to abuse."
The court was told how the abuse of the children by all parties was also evident in text messages.
Watkins sent a text to one of the women saying: "If you belong to me, so does your baby."
In an exchange involving the other woman, she sent Watkins a message along with an image of her child to the effect that her child needed to know she was not loved.

Watkins also planned to "teach" the babies how to take drugs, the hearing was told.
Mr Clee said drugs played "a significant part in his offending against children".
Police found meth, cocaine and GHB during their searches.
Mr Clee told the court drugs were a "regular theme" in his dealings with the two other defendants.
Claiming his innocence, Watkins had told police during interviews he was being stalked by "a crazed fan" and other people had access to his computers.
He claimed he was the "victim of a malicious campaign".
The court heard in Oct 2006, Watkins met up in a hotel with a 16-year-old girl from Boston, who he had met during during a Lostprophets concert.
She dressed in a schoolgirl's outfit and he filmed their encounter.
In Oct 2008 he filmed himself having sex with another 16-year-old girl, who was also a Lostprophets fan.

## Exploited status
One of the two women charged alongside Watkins, Woman A, admitted the attempted rape of a baby after denying rape and two charges of sexual assault as well as taking and distributing an indecent photograph of a child.
Woman B pleaded guilty to conspiring to rape a child, three sexual assault charges and four charges of taking, possessing or distributing indecent images.
After hearing legal argument from barristers, Mr Justice Royce called the jury into court and told them: "There will not be a trial in this case. The defendants have all pleaded guilty to nearly all the charges against them. The prosecution does not seek a trial in these circumstances.
"You have been saved from having to watch extremely graphic and distressing material."
Mr Clee told the judge there had been an argument regarding what some key video evidence showed.
"From the footage, there is an argument as to whether the full offence (of rape) is made out," he told judge Mr Justice Royce.
"If it is made out, it is minimal. There is so little difference between the full attempt and the attempt as to make no difference."

Sally O'Neill, defending Watkins, said the singer was under the care of a psychiatrist.
Speaking outside the court, Det Ch Insp Peter Doyle from South Wales Police said: "This investigation has uncovered the most shocking and harrowing child abuse evidence I have ever seen.
"There is no doubt in my mind that Ian Watkins exploited his celebrity status in order to abuse young children.
"Today's outcome ensures the three people responsible have been brought to justice."
"Two very young children have been removed from this abuse and given a future that would otherwise have been denied them.
"The investigation has been extremely complex and challenging with key information and evidence being identified from witnesses worldwide."
He added that today's guilty pleas did not mark the end of the investigation and the force would work "tirelessly" to identify other victims or witnesses.

HAPPY BIRTHDAY! Michelle Phillips (Rock and Roll Hall of Fame - Mamas & The Papas) (81)
Michelle Gilliam Phillips, born Holly Michelle Gilliam on June 4, 1944, in Long Beach, California, is an American singer, songwriter, and actress best known as a member of the 1960s folk-pop group The Mamas & the Papas. As one of the group's two female vocalists, alongside Cass Elliot, Phillips contributed to their signature harmonies on hits like "California Dreamin’" (1965), "Monday, Monday" (1966), and "Dedicated to the One I Love" (1967). The Mamas & the Papas, formed in 1965 with John Phillips (her then-husband), Denny Doherty, and Elliot, released five studio albums and sold over 40 million records worldwide before disbanding in 1968 due to personal and creative tensions. Phillips co-wrote some of their songs, including "Creeque Alley," which chronicled the band’s origin.

# HAPPY BIRTHDAY! Michelle Phillips... - All Things Music Plus | Facebook
## All Things Music Plus's Post
After the group’s breakup, Phillips pursued acting, appearing in films like Dillinger (1973), earning a Golden Globe nomination, Valentino (1977), and Bloodline (1979), as well as TV shows like Knots Landing and Beverly Hills, 90210. She released a solo album, Victim of Romance (1977), and briefly reunited with The Mamas & the Papas for a 1980s tour. Phillips also co-wrote the song "Kokomo" for The Beach Boys, a No. 1 hit in 1988. She continues to perform occasionally, often with tribute acts, and published a memoir, California Dreamin’: The True Story of The Mamas and the Papas (1986). Phillips was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with the group in 1998.

HAPPY BIRTHDAY! Michelle Phillips (Rock and Roll Hall of Fame - Mamas & The Papas) (81)
Michelle Gilliam Phillips, born Holly Michelle Gilliam on June 4, 1944, in Long Beach, California, is an American singer, songwriter, and actress best known as a member of the 1960s folk-pop group The Mamas & the Papas. As one of the group's two female vocalists, alongside Cass Elliot, Phillips contributed to their signature harmonies on hits like "California Dreamin’" (1965), "Monday, Monday" (1966), and "Dedicated to the One I Love" (1967). The Mamas & the Papas, formed in 1965 with John Phillips (her then-husband), Denny Doherty, and Elliot, released five studio albums and sold over 40 million records worldwide before disbanding in 1968 due to personal and creative tensions. Phillips co-wrote some of their songs, including "Creeque Alley," which chronicled the band’s origin.

**Holly Michelle Phillips** (née **Gilliam**; born June 4, 1944) is an American former singer, songwriter, and actress. Described by _Time_ magazine as the "purest soprano in pop music",[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-lifetime-2) she rose to fame in the mid-1960s with the folk rock vocal group the Mamas & the Papas. After their disbandment, she started a successful acting career in film and television in the 1970s.

A native of Long Beach, California, she spent her early life in Los Angeles and Mexico City, raised by her widowed father. While working as a model in San Francisco, she met and married John Phillips in 1962 and went on to co-found the Mamas & the Papas in 1965. The band rose to fame with their popular singles "[California Dreamin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Dreamin' "California Dreamin'")" and "Creeque Alley", both of which she co-wrote. They released five studio albums before their dissolution in 1970. While married to John Phillips, she gave birth to their daughter, singer Chynna Phillips. Michelle Phillips is the last surviving original member of the band.
After the breakup of the Mamas & the Papas and her divorce from John Phillips, she transitioned into acting, appearing in a supporting part in _The Last Movie_ (1971) before being cast as Billie Frechette in the critically acclaimed crime biopic _Dillinger_ (1973), for which she was nominated for a Golden Globe Award for Most Promising Newcomer. In 1974, she had lead roles in two television films: the crime feature _The Death Squad_, and the teen drama _The California Kid_, in the latter of which she starred opposite Martin Sheen. She went on to appear in a number of films throughout the remainder of the 1970s, including Ken Russell's _Valentino_ (1977), playing Natacha Rambova, and the thriller _Bloodline_ (1979). She released her only solo album, _Victim of Romance_, in 1977.

Phillips's first film of the 1980s was the comedy _[The Man with Bogart's Face](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Man\_with\_Bogart's\_Face "The Man with Bogart's Face")_ (1980). The next year she co-starred with Tom Skerritt in the nature-themed horror _Savage Harvest_ (1981), followed by the television films _Secrets of a Married Man_ (1984) and _The Covenant_ (1985). In 1987, she joined the series _Knots Landing_, portraying Anne Matheson, the mother of Paige Matheson (portrayed by Nicollette Sheridan), until the series's 1993 conclusion.
Phillips later had supporting roles in the comedy film _Let It Ride_ (1989) and the psychological thriller _Scissors_ (1991). In 1998, she was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as a member of the Mamas & the Papas. Phillips appeared in independent films in the 2000s, with supporting parts in _Jane White Is Sick and Twisted_ (2002) and _Kids in America_ (2005) and had recurring guest roles in the television series _[That's Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/That's\_Life\_(2000\_TV\_series) "That's Life (2000 TV series)")_ (2001–2002) and _7th Heaven_ (2001–2004).

Phillips was born Holly Michelle Gilliam on June 4, 1944, in Long Beach, California, the second child of Joyce Leone (née Poole),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-FOOTNOTERiggs2001248-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-4) a Canadian-born accountant, and Gardner Burnett Gilliam,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-gardnerdeath-5) a merchant mariner from San Diego.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-gardnerdeath-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-FOOTNOTEM._Phillips19862-6) She had one older sister, Russell Ann.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-FOOTNOTEM._Phillips19862-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-7) Phillips's paternal grandfather, Marcus Gilliam, was from Walla Walla, Washington,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-8) and worked as a miner and hotelier in Erie, British Columbia.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-nelson-9)Gilliam County, Oregon, takes its name from her paternal ancestors.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-nelson-9) Her mother suffered heart problems stemming from a childhood bout with rheumatic fever, including subacute endocarditis,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-FOOTNOTEM._Phillips19863-10) and died of a related Intracerebral hemorrhage when Phillips was five years old.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-windeler-11) Reflecting on her mother's illness, Phillips said: "They knew it was only a matter of time...

She would lie on the couch in the evenings, listening as my father read to her. One night, after my sister and I had been put to bed, my mother just raised her head, fell unconscious on the couch, and that was it."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-FOOTNOTEM._Phillips19863-10)

### 1965–1969: The Mamas and the Papas
[edit]
Phillips performing with the Mamas & the Papas, circa 1966
The Phillips newlyweds relocated to New York City, where they began writing songs together[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-weller-21) and formed the Mamas and the Papas in 1965.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-26) Michelle co-wrote some of the band's hits, including "[California Dreamin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Dreamin' "California Dreamin'")", which appears on the group's debut album, _If You Can Believe Your Eyes and Ears_ (1966).
Recording of the Mamas and the Papas' second album, titled _The Mamas and the Papas_ (1966) was interrupted when Michelle Phillips' affair with Gene Clark of the Byrds was revealed.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-FOOTNOTEM._Phillips198684%E2%80%9387-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJ._Phillips1986140%E2%80%9348-28) An affair the previous year between Phillips and bandmate Denny Doherty[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGreenwald200291-29) had been forgiven;

### 1965–1969: The Mamas and the Papas
Doherty and John Phillips had reconciled and ostensibly written "I Saw Her Again" (1966) about the episode,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-FOOTNOTEM._Phillips198680%E2%80%9381-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJ._Phillips1986136-31) although they later disagreed about how much Doherty had contributed to the song.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-32) This time, John Phillips was determined to fire his wife.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJ._Phillips1986pp._147-148-33) After consulting their attorney and record label, John Phillips, Cass Elliot, and Denny Doherty served Michelle Phillips with a letter expelling her from the group on June 4, 1966.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-FOOTNOTEM._Phillips198687-34) However, she was rehired on August 23 after the remaining band members concluded that her replacement, Jill Gibson,[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGreenwald2002140-35) lacked her predecessor's "stage charisma and grittier edge".[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJ._Phillips1986203-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-37) After Phillips's reinstatement, the band embarked on a brief tour of the East Coast, playing a series of shows in Washington, D.C., Baltimore,

and at Fordham University in New York City.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGreenwald2002159,_165%E2%80%9367-38)

### 1965–1969: The Mamas and the Papas
In August 1967, the band played what would be their final live performance at the Hollywood Bowl.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGreenwald2002214-41) Phillips would go on to record a fourth and final album with the band, _The Papas & The Mamas_ (1968), before going on a hiatus. In February 1968, she gave birth to their daughter, Chynna Phillips, who later became a vocalist with the 1990s pop trio Wilson Phillips.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWenning1991212-42) Michelle and John, whose marriage was failing at the time, filed for divorce in a Los Angeles County court in May 1969.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-FOOTNOTEM._Phillips198630%E2%80%9332-43) The Mamas and the Papas officially disbanded in 1971 before the release of their final album, _People Like Us_, which was recorded to fulfill contract obligations with their record label.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-ernie-44)

In 1969, while still a member of the Mamas and the Papas, Phillips acted in Gram Parsons's science fiction film _Saturation 70_ alongside Nudie Cohn, Anita Pallenberg, and Julian Jones, the five-year-old son of Rolling Stones guitarist Brian Jones.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-sat-48) The film was never finished, and became a lost film.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-sat-48) The following year, after the breakup of the Mamas and the Papas, she enrolled in acting classes in Los Angeles and has said that she had intended to start her acting career "from scratch", stating that the royalties from the band's records provided her a sustained income while she began to venture into film.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-ernie-44) She studied acting with Peggy Feury.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-buck-49)

Dennis' movie [_The Last Movie_] was a lot of improvisation and craziness."[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-56) Phillips remained a lifelong friend of co-star Stanton.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-57)

During this time, Phillips began dating actor Grainger Hines; she gave birth to their son, Austin Deveraux Hines, on March 3, 1982.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-gritten-69) The following year, she joined the cast of _Hotel_ as the concierge, the daughter of hotel owner Victoria Cabot's rival, who plants his daughter as a spy to further his aim of acquiring control of the St. Gregory. In 1986, she wrote her autobiography, _California Dreamin': The True Story of the Mamas and the Papas_, released just weeks after her former husband's autobiography, _Papa John_.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJ._Phillips1986-73) In it, she describes events such as her first meeting with Cass Elliot; winning 17 straight shoots at a craps table in San Juan, Puerto Rico when the band was broke and could not afford the airfare back to the United States mainland; and how her writing credit on "[California Dreamin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Dreamin' "California Dreamin'")", which still nets her royalties, was "the best wake-up call" she ever had (she was asleep in a New York hotel room when husband John Phillips woke her to help him finish the new song that he was writing).[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-FOOTNOTEM._Phillips198647%E2%80%9355,_64%E2%80%9368-74)

**Holly Michelle Phillips** (née **Gilliam**; born June 4, 1944) is an American former singer, songwriter, and actress. Described by _Time_ magazine as the "purest soprano in pop music",[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-lifetime-2) she rose to fame in the mid-1960s with the folk rock vocal group the Mamas & the Papas. After their disbandment, she started a successful acting career in film and television in the 1970s.

A native of Long Beach, California, she spent her early life in Los Angeles and Mexico City, raised by her widowed father. While working as a model in San Francisco, she met and married John Phillips in 1962 and went on to co-found the Mamas & the Papas in 1965. The band rose to fame with their popular singles "[California Dreamin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Dreamin' "California Dreamin'")" and "Creeque Alley", both of which she co-wrote. They released five studio albums before their dissolution in 1970. While married to John Phillips, she gave birth to their daughter, singer Chynna Phillips. Michelle Phillips is the last surviving original member of the band.
After the breakup of the Mamas & the Papas and her divorce from John Phillips, she transitioned into acting, appearing in a supporting part in _The Last Movie_ (1971) before being cast as Billie Frechette in the critically acclaimed crime biopic _Dillinger_ (1973), for which she was nominated for a Golden Globe Award for Most Promising Newcomer. In 1974, she had lead roles in two television films: the crime feature _The Death Squad_, and the teen drama _The California Kid_, in the latter of which she starred opposite Martin Sheen. She went on to appear in a number of films throughout the remainder of the 1970s, including Ken Russell's _Valentino_ (1977), playing Natacha Rambova, and the thriller _Bloodline_ (1979). She released her only solo album, _Victim of Romance_, in 1977.

Phillips claimed she got cast by pretending to be half Cherokee, like her character.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-52) The film was critically acclaimed, and _Variety_ said of her performance: "Phillips, making her film bow after having been a member of the Mamas & the Papas singing group, scores heavily as Dillinger's girlfriend",[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-53) while the _New York Times_ noted it as "mildly effective".[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-54) Phillips was nominated for a Golden Globe Award for Most Promising Newcomer for her performance.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-goldenglobe-55) Reflecting on the film, Phillips said: "I was so lucky to have been surrounded by really great actors. Everybody in that movie was a real actor: Warren Oates, Ben Johnson, Cloris Leachman, Richard Dreyfuss, Harry Dean Stanton. It was just a wonderful, wonderful experience for me and I had so much support and so much help and so much encouragement. That was really my first movie.

### 1977–1986: Solo album, film, and writing
[edit]
Phillips at the 1971 Golden Globe Awards
In 1977, Phillips released her only solo album, _Victim of Romance_, produced by Jack Nitzsche for A&M Records.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-60) Commenting on the record, she said: "I didn't do it earlier because I never felt secure enough as a vocalist. I'm good, but Cass was always better." Phillips also commented on her involvement in its production, saying that she had been involved in "every aspect, from mixing to putting together the package and cover myself".[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-crowe-51) Her first two solo singles from the album failed to make the U.S. music charts. Concurrent with her solo album release, she sang backup vocals with former stepdaughter Mackenzie Phillips on "Zulu Warrior" for her ex-husband's second solo album, _Pay Pack & Follow_. Around the same time, she starred as Rudolph Valentino's second wife Natacha Rambova in Ken Russell's film _Valentino_ (1977). The film received mixed reviews, with _Time Out_ London saying: "Structured as a series of flashbacks from Valentino's funeral to his early years in America, the first hour or so of this biopic is Russell's sanest and most controlled work in several years, despite its hollow cynicism."[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-61) The following year, Phillips married radio executive Robert Burch,[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-62) though their marriage ended in 1979.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-Jerome-63)

In 1979, she appeared in the film adaptation of the Sidney Sheldon novel _Bloodline_ (1979), a thriller starring Audrey Hepburn and Ben Gazzara. Released in June 1979, _Bloodline_ received negative reviews from critics,[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-64) and Phillips's performance (along with those of James Mason and Maurice Ronet) was criticized by _Variety_ as being "drab".[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-65) The same year, she recorded the song _Forever_ for the movie soundtrack of _California Dreaming_, a surf film unrelated to her former group despite its title.
Phillips in 1979
Phillips' other film credits during this period include roles in the comedy _[The Man with Bogart's Face](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Man\_with\_Bogart's\_Face "The Man with Bogart's Face")_ (1980),[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-66) the nature horror film _Savage Harvest_ (1981), about a family being attacked by a pride of lions,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-67) and _American Anthem_ (1986). On television, Phillips played the mermaid princess Nyah in three episodes of _Fantasy Island_ and Leora Van Treas in _Mike Hammer: Murder Takes All_ (1983), starring Stacy Keach in the title role.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-68) She appeared in TV miniseries such as _Aspen_ (1977) and _The French Atlantic Affair_ (1979).

In 1986, she wrote her autobiography, _California Dreamin': The True Story of the Mamas and the Papas_, released just weeks after her former husband's autobiography, _Papa John_.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJ._Phillips1986-73) In it, she describes events such as her first meeting with Cass Elliot; winning 17 straight shoots at a craps table in San Juan, Puerto Rico when the band was broke and could not afford the airfare back to the United States mainland; and how her writing credit on "[California Dreamin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Dreamin' "California Dreamin'")", which still nets her royalties, was "the best wake-up call" she ever had (she was asleep in a New York hotel room when husband John Phillips woke her to help him finish the new song that he was writing).[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Phillips#cite_note-FOOTNOTEM._Phillips198647%E2%80%9355,_64%E2%80%9368-74)
